title: Counting Methods
weightage: Medium — combinations and the counting principle appear regularly and feed directly into probability
intro: Counting is the engine room of probability, and the GRE tests it in its own right too. The whole subject rests on one idea — the counting (multiplication) principle — and two specialisations of it: permutations, where order matters, and combinations, where it does not. The single decision that determines almost every answer is whether arrangement counts: choosing 3 people for a committee is a combination, but seating 3 people in a row is a permutation. The GRE keeps the numbers small enough to reason through, so you rarely need a calculator; what it rewards is setting up the count correctly and, above all, not overcounting. Get the order-matters question right and handle restrictions cleanly, and this becomes one of the more mechanical, dependable topics on the test.

items.name: Counting principle
items.formula: if step 1 has m ways and step 2 has n ways, together m × n ways

items.name: Circular arrangements
items.formula: (n − 1)! ways to seat n around a round table

topics.name: The Counting Principle
topics.details: The fundamental counting principle says that if one choice can be made in m ways and an independent following choice in n ways, the two together can be made in m × n ways — and this extends to any number of stages. A meal with 4 mains and 3 desserts offers 4 × 3 = 12 combinations; a 3-character code from 26 letters (repeats allowed) offers 26 × 26 × 26 outcomes. The key word is independent: multiply when each stage's options do not depend on the previous choice. When repetition is not allowed, the pool shrinks by one at each stage — a first digit from 5 options, then 4, then 3. And when the task splits into mutually exclusive cases ("the code starts with a vowel OR a digit"), you add the case counts rather than multiply. Deciding multiply-vs-add is the whole skill: multiply across independent stages of one arrangement, add across separate scenarios.

solved.problem: A café offers 4 sandwiches, 3 drinks and 2 desserts. How many different meals of one each?
How many 3-letter codes can be formed from the 26 letters if repetition is allowed?
solved.solution: Each of the 3 positions has 26 options: 26 × 26 × 26 = 17,576.

solved.problem: How many 3-digit numbers have all distinct digits and no leading zero?
solved.solution: Hundreds digit: 9 options (1–9). Tens: 9 left (0–9 minus the one used). Units: 8 left. 9 × 9 × 8 = 648.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: the number of 2-letter codes from {A,B,C,D} with repetition allowed. Quantity B: the number of 2-letter codes from {A,B,C,D,E} with no repetition. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Quantity A = 4 × 4 = 16. Quantity B = 5 × 4 = 20. Quantity B is greater.

unsolved.problem: A wardrobe has 5 shirts and 4 pairs of trousers. How many shirt-trouser outfits?
How many 4-digit PINs are possible (digits 0–9, repetition allowed)?
How many 2-digit numbers have distinct digits and no leading zero?
A quiz has 3 true/false questions. How many ways to answer all three?
A license plate is 2 letters then 3 digits, repetition allowed. How many plates?

topics.name: Permutations
topics.details: A permutation counts arrangements where order matters. Arranging r items chosen from n distinct items gives nPr = n!/(n−r)! — which is just the counting principle applied to shrinking choices: n for the first slot, n−1 for the second, and so on for r slots. Seating, ranking, forming ordered codes from distinct symbols, and awarding distinct positions (gold/silver/bronze) are all permutations. Two special cases show up often. When some items repeat, divide by the factorial of each repeat count: the arrangements of the letters in LEVEL are 5!/(2!·2!) = 30, because the two L's and two E's are indistinguishable. When items are arranged in a circle, fix one item to kill rotational duplicates, giving (n−1)! arrangements. The GRE keeps n small, so the arithmetic is light — the discipline is recognising that order counts before you reach for a formula.

solved.problem: In how many ways can 5 distinct books be arranged on a shelf?
From 7 runners, in how many ways can gold, silver and bronze be awarded?
How many distinct arrangements of the letters in the word LEVEL are there?
solved.solution: 5 letters with two L's and two E's: 5!/(2!·2!) = 120/4 = 30.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: the number of ways to seat 4 people in a row. Quantity B: the number of ways to seat 4 people around a round table. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Row: 4! = 24. Round table: (4−1)! = 3! = 6 (rotations are identical). Quantity A (24) > Quantity B (6). Answer: A is greater.

unsolved.problem: In how many ways can 4 distinct paintings be hung in a row?
From 6 candidates, how many ways to choose a president and a vice-president?
How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BOOK?
In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table?
How many 3-digit numbers use each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 at most once?

topics.name: Combinations
topics.details: A combination counts selections where order does not matter. Choosing r items from n distinct items gives nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!]. The clean way to see it: count the ordered arrangements (nPr) then divide by r! to erase the orderings of the same group, since {A,B,C} and {C,B,A} are one committee, not six. Combinations govern committees, teams, handshakes, choosing pizza toppings, and drawing a group of cards. Two facts save time. First, the symmetry nCr = nC(n−r): choosing 8 of 10 to include is the same as choosing 2 of 10 to leave out, so compute the easier one. Second, nC0 = nCn = 1 and nC1 = n. The pivotal GRE decision remains order: "how many ways to pick 3 people for a team" is a combination (15 or 20-ish, small), while "how many ways to assign 3 distinct offices" is a permutation (larger). If swapping two chosen items produces a genuinely different outcome, it is a permutation; if not, a combination.

solved.problem: How many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 8 people?
At a party of 6 people, everyone shakes hands once with everyone else. How many handshakes?
solved.solution: Each handshake is a pair, order irrelevant: 6C2 = (6×5)/2 = 15.

solved.problem: A pizza shop has 7 toppings. How many ways to choose exactly 5 toppings?
Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: the number of ways to choose 2 people from 5. Quantity B: the number of ways to arrange 2 people from 5 in order. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Quantity A = 5C2 = 10. Quantity B = 5P2 = 20. Ordering doubles the count (divide by 2! to go from B to A). Quantity B is greater.

unsolved.problem: How many ways to choose 2 books from 6 to take on a trip?
From 10 employees, how many 4-person teams can be formed?
A student must pick 3 electives from 9. How many selections?
How many ways to choose 5 cards from a set of 6 distinct cards?
hints: Choosing 5 to keep = choosing 1 to drop.

unsolved.problem: In a group of 8, how many distinct pairs can be formed?

topics.name: Overcounting & Restrictions
topics.details: The hardest counting questions add a twist that makes the naïve product wrong, and there are three reliable repair tools. First, the complement: to count arrangements with "at least one" of something, count the total and subtract the arrangements with none — usually far faster than adding cases. Second, glue and treat as a block: when items must sit together, bind them into one unit, arrange the units, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the block. Third, handle the restricted slot first: if a code cannot start with 0, choose the first position from its allowed options before filling the rest. The deepest idea is overcounting — whenever your method counts each valid outcome more than once, divide by the size of that repeat. This is exactly why combinations divide permutations by r!, and why a round table divides by n. The moment a scenario feels like it double-counts, ask "by what factor?" and divide.

solved.problem: How many ways can 5 people be arranged in a row if two particular people, A and B, must sit together?
solved.solution: Glue A and B into one block: arrange 4 units in 4! = 24 ways, then order A and B inside the block in 2! = 2 ways. Total = 24 × 2 = 48.

solved.problem: From tossing a coin 3 times, in how many ways do you get at least one head?
solved.solution: Total outcomes = 2³ = 8. The only outcome with no head is TTT (1 way). At least one head = 8 − 1 = 7.

solved.problem: How many 3-digit numbers (no leading zero) can be formed from digits 0–9 with no repeated digit, and must be even?
solved.solution: Split by the units digit. Units = 0: hundreds 9, tens 8 → 72. Units ∈ {2,4,6,8} (4 choices): hundreds cannot be 0 or the units digit → 8 options; tens = 8 remaining → 4 × 8 × 8 = 256. Total = 72 + 256 = 328.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. 4 people sit in a row. Quantity A: arrangements where two specific people sit together. Quantity B: arrangements where they do NOT sit together. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Total = 4! = 24. Together (block method): 3! × 2! = 12. Not together = 24 − 12 = 12. Quantity A = Quantity B = 12. Answer: the two are equal.

unsolved.problem: How many ways can 4 books be arranged so that 2 specific books are next to each other?
hints: Glue the two into one block.
Arrange 3 units: 3!, then order the block: 2!.

unsolved.problem: Rolling a die once, how many outcomes are "not a 6"?
From 5 people, how many ways to line up all 5 if one specific person must be first?
Tossing a coin 4 times, how many outcomes have at least one tail?
How many 3-letter arrangements of A, B, C, D never start with A?
hints: Count those that DO start with A: fix A, arrange 2 of remaining 3.

shortcuts: Decide order first: order matters → permutation (nPr); order does not → combination (nCr). This one call fixes most problems.
Multiply across independent stages of one arrangement; ADD across separate mutually exclusive cases.
Use symmetry nCr = nC(n−r) to compute the smaller side — 20C18 is just 20C2 = 190.
For "at least one", count the complement (none) and subtract from the total.
For "must sit together", glue the items into a block, arrange, then multiply by the block's internal orderings.
Round-table seatings of n items = (n−1)!, because rotations repeat.
The GRE keeps n small — a basic calculator is enough; the setup, not the arithmetic, is the challenge.
mistakes: Using a permutation when order does not matter (or a combination when it does) — the single biggest counting error.
Multiplying when the scenarios are separate cases that should be added.
Forgetting to divide out repeats — arrangements of BOOK are 4!/2!, not 4!.
Ignoring a leading-zero or other restriction and filling positions left-to-right blindly.
Double-counting a group as several ordered lists (that is exactly what dividing by r! prevents).
Treating a circular arrangement like a row and using n! instead of (n−1)!.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — Column A: 6C2. Column B: 6C4. Which is greater?
Concept — How many ways can a 4-person committee be chosen from 9 people?
pyq.a: 9C4 = 126. Order does not matter, so it is a combination.

pyq.q: Numeric Entry — In how many ways can the letters of the word ERROR be arranged?
Multiple-answer — Which situations are permutations (order matters)? (seating in a row / choosing a committee / awarding 1st-2nd-3rd / forming a 3-digit code from distinct digits)
pyq.a: Seating in a row, awarding 1st-2nd-3rd, and forming an ordered code — all care about order. Choosing a committee does not.

flashcards.back: multiply the options across independent stages
glue as a block, arrange, × internal orderings

summary: Everything builds on the counting principle: multiply options across independent stages.
Order matters → permutation nPr; order does not → combination nCr = nPr divided by r!.
Add across separate cases; multiply across stages of a single arrangement.
Divide out repeats — that is the cure for overcounting, and why combinations and circles divide.
Use nCr = nC(n−r) to compute the easier side.
For "at least one", subtract the complement from the total.
For "must sit together", glue into a block, arrange the units, then order within the block.
The GRE keeps the numbers small — correct setup beats fast arithmetic every time.
